Today we are announcing our biggest bet yet on our own silicon. Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services. And we’re introducing Maia 300, which delivers 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems. We are already deploying Maia 200 across the US, Europe, and Australia, delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt across experiences in Teams and Copilot. Our goal is to build on the full-stack efficiency gains we’ve already seen, while continuing to bring the latest innovations from across the ecosystem into our fleet. 40% more tokens per watt, but at what context length? The workloads you named, sustained multi-step agents, carry long contexts, and every agent's working memory grows with each step. At that point the binding constraint is memory, not compute, and the specs that lead this launch are memory specs. Tokens per watt measured on short contexts says little about tokens per watt once agent memory dominates. The bigger announcement may be co-design. With Maia as the primary engine, Copilot's models get shaped around Maia and each next Maia around Copilot's workloads. That's where the gain compounds, and it's very hard to copy from outside. It also splits the market: integrated model-plus-chip stacks on one side, open models on general-purpose GPUs on the other. As agents multiply token demand, that gap becomes the price difference between closed and open AI. Who gives open models what Maia gives Copilot?

[Isabella Marino](https://au.linkedin.com/in/isabella-marino-692454439?trk=public_post_comment_actor-name) 4w


The question that sits underneath the announcement is not about efficiency. You are about to run multi-gigawatt inference for agents that act — that buy, sign, dispatch, approve, execute — across Teams, Copilot, and the Azure estate. Every one of those actions will commit against a real target at some point. The tokens-per-watt number tells us how cheap the compute is. It does not tell us what stands between an agent's decision and the consequence when the agent has valid credentials, valid authority, and intent to exceed scope. The industry has spent two years building the layer above the action: monitoring, containment, audit, oversight. Every incident in that window had the same shape. The credentials were valid. The policy was configured. The action fired anyway. Whoever solves that layer first owns the next decade of enterprise AI. It is not the model layer, it is not the silicon layer, and it is not the SaaS layer. It is the layer between the decision and the consequence. You have the biggest bet on the silicon. That is the correct place to be building. But the layer that makes agents safe to run at scale is not on the roadmap you just published.
